title: mixed-seqlen-residue-pinning-playbook
content:
Summary

This is a working playbook capturing experiments and hypotheses from the mixed sequence-length (mixed-seqlen) regression we’ve been seeing in production: sudden tail-latency spikes and elevated NVMe paging when short interactive requests co-exist with long batch/stream requests. The goal is to: (1) quantify the root cause at the KV cache level (reuse vs residency), (2) test mitigations that are low-risk for rollout, and (3) produce a repeatable benchmark harness.

Motivation / problem statement

- Symptoms observed: transient 99.9th token latency jumps (+60–120 ms), concurrent increase in page-out events and a >20% drop in measured per-GPU memory bandwidth headroom during surges.
- Affected config: multi-tenant serving nodes running model-family X (decoder-only), standard TTL-based residency with global LRU-ish eviction and no bank-awareness.
- Suspected mechanism: long-request KV footprints cause bank/channel saturation and push short-request hot prefixes out; short prefixes are then re-requested after a tiny gap causing microburst re-warm and repeated NVMe reads (read amplification).

Hypotheses

H1: High-seqlen requests pin a lot of distinct KV pages across many banks, reducing effective resident capacity for hot prefixes used by short requests.
H2: Global LRU eviction combined with aggressive prefetch for long requests causes churn (hot prefixes evicted shortly after access → low reuse despite recent use).
H3: Memory channel saturation (bank skew) increases NVMe read latency for spillback, amplifying tail effects even when average bandwidth looks OK.

Experiment plan overview

A. Microbench harness (controlled):
  - Synthetic workload generator which emits two poisson-arrival streams: short (mean seq 32, p95 latency target) and long (mean seq 1024), with tunable relative QPS.
  - Trace collection: per-request KV page list, per-page last-touch timestamp, eviction decisions, NVMe page-out/in events, per-bank request counters, and perf counters for memory BW.
  - Targets: measure reuse_rate (fraction of accesses hitting resident KV), eviction_rate (evicts/sec), page_out_rate, and tail token latency.

B. Field trace replay: replay real production traces but annotate by seqlen to reproduce in staging cluster.

C. Mitigations to try (in parallel experiments):
  1) Short-prefix pin set: keep a small FIFO pin set for prefixes shorter than configurable threshold (e.g., seq<=64). Aim: protect short-hot keys from being evicted by long requests.
  2) Bank-aware allocation: when allocating pages for long requests, prefer banks with free headroom or use spread factor that avoids concentrating on a few banks.
  3) Decay-window LRU: make recency decay slower for short-request keys (hybrid aging).
  4) Prefetch limiter for long requests: reduce prefetch depth when node BW utilization > threshold.
  5) Spill QoS: deprioritize NVMe reads spawned by long requests under burst conditions (risk: increases cold tail latency for long requests).

Benchmark config and hardware

- Node: rGPU-8 (A100x8 equivalent), 1 TB host DRAM, local NVMe raid0 (2x2TB), PCIe 4.0.
- Serving runtime build: main@6d2f9a + band-aware-prefetch branch modifications.
- Model: family X 8B dense, KV pages ~2 KiB per token window (estimated).
- Workload mixes: short-only, long-only, 80/20, 50/50, 20/80 (short/long by QPS).
- Observation windows: steady-state 15 minutes + 10-minute surge phases.

Key metrics to capture (definitions)

- reuse_rate: count(resident hits) / count(total kv accesses) over sliding 30s windows.
- eviction_rate: evictions/sec reported by eviction worker.
- page_out_rate: NVMe page-out requests/sec.
- bw_headroom: aggregate memory channel bandwidth spare capacity (perf counter-derived) as percentage.
- tail_token_latency_ms: 99th/99.9th of token generation time per request.

Preliminary runs and notable numbers (summary)

- Baseline 50/50 mix: reuse_rate ~ 0.72 overall; short-request reuse_rate ~0.42; eviction_rate ~820/s; page_out_rate ~180/s during surge; bw_headroom dropped from 44% -> 12% at surge peak; tail_token_99.9 ~ +95ms over short-only baseline.
- Short-pin experiment (pin set size = 8K prefixes): short-request reuse_rate rose to ~0.86, eviction_rate fell to ~540/s, page_out_rate fell to 96/s; tail_token_99.9 reduced to +20ms. Long-request median token latency increased ~6% (acceptable for our SLOs).
- Bank-aware allocation prototype: reduced bank skew metric (stddev of per-bank occupancy) by ~38%, page_out_rate fell 22%, but implementation added ~4% allocation overhead.
- Prefetch limiter: aggressive prefetch cutoff at BW>65% avoided many page-outs; however, it slightly increased cold-start latency for long batched streams (~12%).

Observations / interpretation

- The dominant factor appears to be contention at memory channel/bank level rather than pure global capacity shortfall. Long requests scatter across many banks and when they are dense they saturate channels, which delays NVMe service and causes ripple eviction decisions to be more damaging.
- Short-prefixes are highly recoverable if we protect them by small pins; they have high reuse but low resident footprint.
- Prefetch heuristics tuned to ignore bandwidth signals can worsen the situation — prefetch is powerful but needs to respect BW QoS.

Risks and tradeoffs

- Pinning increases resident set and reduces headroom for long requests; needs upper bound and adaptive admission.
- Bank-aware allocation can reduce tail but adds allocator complexity and CPU overhead — must be measured for cost.
- Spill QoS helps tails for short requests but may visibly harm throughput for long batch jobs (potentially acceptable if long jobs are non-latency-critical).

Proposed short-term rollout plan (safe path)

1) Implement short-prefix pinning as an opt-in config in staging with: max_pin_entries=8k, pin_ttl=300s, only for prefixes with seq<=64.
2) Add a bandwidth probe and prefetch limiter: when bw_headroom < 25% disable speculative prefetch for requests with seq > 256.
3) Deploy to a small canary fleet (2 nodes) with synthetic 50/50 mixed load and run 48hr soak. Monitor: short reuse_rate, page_out_rate, tail_token_99.9, long_request_median_latency.
4) If canary looks good, expand to 10% of serving nodes and gate on customer-impact telemetry.

Instrumentation additions (must-haves)

- Per-page bank id added to traces.
- Per-eviction decision reason (capacity vs bank_pressure vs age) exported into traces.
- Lightweight allocation histogram per-bank (1s resolution).
- NVMe latency tail histograms by request type (short vs long).

Open questions / TODOs

- What is a safe default for max_pin_entries for different node sizes? (Param sweep required across rGPU-4/8/16).
- Should pinning be per-tenant or global? Multi-tenant fairness concerns.
- How to reconcile pin admission with Dedicated customer isolation guarantees? (security/ops review).
- Need perf regression tests for allocator overhead and prefetch limiter CPU impact.

Actions / next experiments

- Diego: add per-page bank id and eviction_reason to trace events (ENG-1428) — due 2024-10-14.
- Priya: spin up synthetic harness with configurable seqlen mix and run batch of sweeps for max_pin_entries {2k,4k,8k,16k} across rGPU-4/8 — due 2024-10-18.
- Tomas: prototype bank-aware allocation fallback inside allocator (branch: bank-alloc-proto) — due 2024-10-21.
- Ava: coordinate canary rollout config and build the dashboard (short vs long latency, reuse, pageouts) — due 2024-10-25.

Notes to self / rough ideas

- Consider metric: microburst_rewarm_count = number of page-ins for a prefix within T seconds after eviction; more actionable than raw page_out_rate.
- Evaluate probabilistic pinning (sample-based keep) to bound tail-case worst resident size.
- If bank-aware allocation is expensive, consider lazy remap where we opportunistically migrate a subset of pages off hot banks during idle cycles.

References and links

- Slack thread: #serving-runtime > thread: mixed-seqlen tail analysis (link omitted)
- Related tickets: ENG-1259 (prefetch QoS infra), ENG-1382 (NVMe tail mitigation), ENG-1428 (trace enrichment)
